mcqs.question: In the expand-then-shrink template for a longest-valid-window problem, what triggers the inner while loop to execute?
options: It runs unconditionally exactly once per outer loop iteration
It runs only once the right pointer reaches the end of the array
The window becoming invalid as a direct result of the most recent expansion
The value at the right pointer being smaller than the value at the left pointer
mcqs.explanation: The inner loop's only job is to restore validity after an expansion just broke it — it may run zero, one, or several times depending on how invalid the window became, not on a fixed schedule tied to the outer loop or to comparing specific values.

mcqs.question: In Longest Substring Without Repeating Characters, why must the duplicate-removal step be a while loop rather than an if statement?
options: An if statement would behave identically, since a violation is always caused by exactly the leftmost element in the window
An if statement is required instead of while specifically to avoid an infinite loop in this algorithm
The while loop keeps removing elements from the left until the actual duplicate character is gone, which can take more than one removal
A while loop is only necessary when the string mixes uppercase and lowercase letters
mcqs.explanation: Depending on how far left has fallen behind due to earlier shrinks, expelling one specific duplicate character can require removing several elements in sequence — a single if would leave the window still invalid after one removal in exactly that case. It has nothing to do with letter casing, and an if would not cause an infinite loop; it would simply under-correct.

mcqs.question: In Smallest Subarray With Sum At Least Target, why does the code record `best` on every iteration of the shrink while-loop, rather than once after the loop exits?
options: Because the sum could still be below target once the loop exits, so recording then would capture an invalid window
Each shrink step produces a new, still-valid, strictly smaller window — recording only the first or last one would miss shorter valid windows found in between
Recording once after the loop exits is a standard optimization that yields the identical minimum faster
best only needs to be recorded the very first time the window becomes valid at all
mcqs.explanation: Every pass through the while body represents a genuinely valid, progressively smaller window, and any of them could be the true minimum — checking only the boundary points of the shrink sequence would silently skip the smallest one in the middle. The loop exits precisely when the window is no longer valid, so recording after exit would use invalid data, not save time.

mcqs.question: Replacing the shrink loop's `while` with an `if` in a variable-window solution causes what kind of failure?
options: A guaranteed infinite loop that never terminates
A compile-time type error in most mainstream languages
The window can remain invalid after only a single shrink step, since one removal might not fully restore validity, silently corrupting later checks
No observable difference, since every variable-window problem only ever needs at most one shrink step
mcqs.explanation: Some invalidity states require more than one element removed from the left before the window is genuinely valid again — an if only performs one removal, leaving the window in a broken state that subsequent iterations then operate on as if it were valid. This doesn't loop forever or fail to compile; it produces a plausible but wrong answer.

mcqs.question: Why does prefix-sum-plus-hashmap handle negative values correctly for sum-based subarray problems where the variable-size sliding window can't?
options: Because hashmaps are inherently more numerically precise with negative values than plain arrays
The sliding window's shrink logic assumes the running sum only ever increases as the window grows, which breaks once negative values can decrease it — the hashmap approach makes no such assumption
Because prefix sums are mathematically guaranteed to stay non-negative for any input array
Because the sliding-window technique cannot be implemented at all on arrays containing negative numbers
mcqs.explanation: The window's 'shrink while sum ≥ target' logic is only safe because growing the window monotonically increases the sum with non-negative values — negatives can make the sum drop as the window grows, so a window that looked invalid could become valid later without shrinking, which the greedy shrink logic never accounts for. Prefix-sum-plus-hashmap doesn't rely on that monotonicity at all, and it's unrelated to numeric precision or sign of the prefix sums themselves.
